elements.text: Matter is particulate: spaces, motion, and attraction govern all physical states.

items.meaning: Particles have intermolecular spaces; sugar particles fit between water particles.
Particles possess kinetic energy; motion increases as temperature rises (diffusion).
Intermolecular attractive forces hold particles together; strength varies by substance.

beats.narration: Take a 100 mL beaker, fill it half with water, and mark the initial water level carefully with a pen.
Now add two spoonfuls of sugar and stir thoroughly with a glass rod until every single crystal dissolves completely.
Look closely at the water mark again. Did the water level rise? No! It stays exactly where it was.
Why? Where did all that solid sugar go?
Water is not a solid continuous block. It is made of millions of tiny particles with empty spaces between them.
When sugar dissolves, its individual particles break away and get into the spaces between the water particles.
Think of an unlit incense stick lying in the corner of a room. To smell it, you have to bring your nose right up to it.
Now light the tip. Within seconds, the fragrance reaches you sitting all the way across the room.
The fragrant vapour particles possess kinetic energy. They move constantly in all directions and intermix on their own with the particles of air.
This spontaneous intermixing of particles of two different types of matter on their own is called diffusion.
What happens if we heat a substance? As temperature rises, particles gain more kinetic energy and move faster, so diffusion speeds up.
Look at these three objects: an iron nail, a piece of chalk, and a rubber band. Let's try to break them by hammering, pulling, or cutting.
The chalk breaks easily into small powder with a light hit of a hammer.
The rubber band stretches when pulled and snaps back, needing more force to break.
The iron nail does not break at all even under heavy hammering.
Why this difference? Particles of matter have an attractive force acting between them that keeps them together.
The strength of this force of attraction varies from one substance to another.
Let us bring together the three fundamental properties we discovered today in our notebook.
Remember: in solids, spaces are minimum and attraction is maximum. In gases, spaces are maximum and attraction is minimum.
These three simple rules explain how everything around you—solid ice, liquid water, and steam—behaves!
